segments.text: Senator Holch, thank you for making time
for us.
>> Of course.
>> Yeah, for this for this run. You know,
we're just a few weeks out until
Kansans go to vote on the next governor
as well as senator and everything else
that we're seeing. So, question for you
is how to win on this because we're
predominantly Republican state, often
see this for statewide elections, but
not for governor as you well know.
In 2018, Governor Laura Kelly won nine
counties including Sedgwick County, also
Harvey County which is just to the north
of us.
Also won in 2022 eight counties. Is the
math similar for you on this approach?
And I imagine you're going to say, well,
you know, I want to be the governor for
all Kansans. But realistically, when you
add up all those counties, Johnson 27%,
Sedgwick 16, Shawnee which is Topeka
seven, Douglas Lawrence five. That's
about 55% of the electorate that's out
there. How important is it for you to
perform very well in these counties and
then probably hold down the margins
elsewhere?
>> Yeah, it's absolutely important. I mean,
obviously the concentration of
population is towards the eastern side.
So, of course a lot of focus there.
However, um,
you know, you want to make sure that
you're serving all of Kansas and that's
why I started this 16 months ago in
terms of making sure that I was getting
out across the state to different areas,
western, eastern, central, all over the
place. So, um, but you know,
mathematically you're absolutely right
that, you know, that concentration again
is on the eastern side. However, I'm
from a rural area. I know what it's like
to be in those areas. You want to be
seen and heard and that's why also I've
put, you know, so much emphasis on
making sure I'm making those stops in
western Kansas and listening to the
folks and what their needs are.
>> So, we've seen this for the past eight
years with Governor Kelly in office and
I'm seeing just by this Democrats would
have to flip four seats in the Senate,
five in the House in the supermajority
that Republicans have. If you win in
November, Senator, how can you be
effective even if there's still a
supermajority in place and you're not
just a symbolic veto?
>> Yeah, I've been effective. In fact, I'm
the most successful Democrat in the
Senate in terms of getting bills
implemented and actually more successful
than 90% of the Republicans in getting
bills and ideas implemented. So,
um I have a history of being able to
work collaboratively. That started back
when I first came into the legislature
and was a co-founder of the women's
bipartisan caucus. We're the group that
actually put together the bill that
ended the Brownback experiment to get us
back on track to better fund our schools
and roads and highways and critical
infrastructure. So, I have that history
of working collaboratively with folks
across uh the aisle. That will continue
in terms of setting the stage of how
we're going to work. Granted, I will
tell you, you know, be thrilled to flip
some of those seats out there because
you know, it takes a lot of energy. It
takes a lot of work to rain to get more
people on board from across the aisle
often. You know, if we had a bigger
number of Democrats, moderate
Republicans working together towards the
same goal, you know, that makes a little
bit easier, of course.
>> Time for the labeling part of our
interview for this.
>> Yeah.
>> And we'll get into the state fair in
just a moment. But [snorts] when you see
this right now, we have 65 counties in
our viewing area. 63, 64 of them are
likely to vote Republican if you're
going past the history. Sedgwick County,
successful Democrats have won Sedgwick
County.
Nearly all the attack ads, and I'm out
here anchoring 4 hours of news a day.
>> Right.
>> I pretty much see every commercial
break, maybe 25 commercial breaks a day.
Nearly every single one of them says
liberal Cindy Holscher.
So, using Governor Kelly and before that
Governor Kathleen Sebelius, Democrats
who won statewide and Sebelius had real
margin in her victories, where do you
align yourself politically comparing
yourself to the two of them? So, if
we're going on left over here, right all
the way over here, where is Cindy
Holscher in comparison to where Kathleen
Sebelius was, where Governor Kelly is?
>> Yeah. Like most Kansans, I'm right there
in the middle. I'm very mainstream. And
you know, every election I've had uh all
four prior to this,
I have had that label attached to me by
uh my
my opponents.
They're always saying radical liberal
things like that, but it can't be true
because keep in mind every election I've
had prior to this one, all four of them,
were in red districts. Republicans have
been electing me. And you know, they
wouldn't be electing me if I were
actually extreme
or any of those labels that, you know,
that's the that's the thing I always say
that opponents do when they don't have
anything else. They start putting labels
out there. So, again, keep in mind every
one of my elections as a Democrat has
been in a red area where Republicans are
electing me. They wouldn't keep doing
that if I wasn't mainstream.
>> Let's go deeper on the labeling. So,
state fair debate, I've spent last few
days really breaking it down. September
12th, hot day in Hutchinson, Kansas,
just a scosh, right? There was a lot of
yelling over 90 minutes, and you got the
crowd there, so I can understand playing
to some of the crowd, but so for your
opponent, Senator Ty Masterson, I
counted you referencing him as Brownback
or Brownback 2.0, the former governor,
six times. Two referencing the no-show
job for Masterson and the claims of that
three times at GoCreate Wichita State.
Four references for your own campaign,
working families. Four references to
billionaires, of which my research shows
we have a grand total of five of those
in Kansas, and one of those, Charles
Koch, could buy the other four three
times over. But do you think the
narrative of your opponents
will help in our viewing area
to try to close some of that gap that we
see in the rural counties because
there's such a heavy attack at present
against you right now. But to try to say
whatever you can about Senator Masterson
and for places that typically vote
Republican to try to see if you can get
some doubt in their mind?
>> Mhm. Mhm. Well, here's what I know.
Brownback experiment, I mean, we've been
taking the past 8 years to crawl out of
it
with the leadership of Governor Kelly.
We've made progress. There's still, you
know, ways to go, but boy, I mean, it
hurt us. It hurt us hard, and that was
people all across the state in terms of
our schools, our roads and highways, and
important agencies being defunded. So,
you know,
uh the the feelings are still there and
there's a large group of people that it
wasn't that long ago in terms of the
effects and we're still getting over it.
So, absolutely that resonates with them.
But, to me the bigger thing too there
that you mentioned is the fact that, you
know, we have a lot of folks across the
state working two and three jobs just
trying to get by.
Yet, we have Senator Masterson who has a
no-show job, has collected over a
million dollars for a job he hasn't had
to show up to, while we have people all
across the state, so many of us
struggling just to get by.
That's unfair and it feels corrupt and I
understand why people,
um you know, are very anxious about the
future and and don't like what they're
seeing and what they're hearing when we
have the person a person running for
governor
who literally is collecting a nice
salary through the legislature, but then
additional salary for not even showing
up for a job.
>> We'll talk about affordability later on
this. We're going to keep with the
labeling, but now we're going to flip
it. Now, to what Senator Masterson
called you and Hutchinson.
Radical liberal socialist Democrat six
times. He called you just a socialist
seven times. Going to turn Kansas into
California three times. So, I'm going to
give you the chance to answer back on
this, but also and I will ask Senator
Masterson the same thing if he
interviews with us.
Do Kansans deserve better than what we
saw at the state fair when it comes to
just labeling and actually talking a lot
of policy? Cuz there wasn't a lot of
time for that and I can understand that
because you got the heat, you got the
crowd and everything else. But, for all
those labels, the socialist label, the
turning Kansas into California, I'm
going to give you a chance to respond to
that.
>> Kansans absolutely deserve better and
I'm ready to show up and do more
debates.
Um some in studios like this one where
there wouldn't be an audience.
But, no-show Masterson doesn't plan to
show up not only for that job, but
doesn't plan to show up for any more
debates. I'm ready to go. I'm ready to
talk policy and let's talk a little bit
of policy there. Again, with those
labels, here are the things I'm fighting
for. Medicaid expansion,
funding of our schools, legalizing
cannabis, access to affordable housing,
lowering property taxes. You know what?
Over 65%
of the population supports those things.
I'm not extreme. I'm mainstream. Now,
Senator Masterson, he's on the opposite
side of all of those issues. Stopping
Medicaid expansion, trying to defund our
schools, has literally been the person
stopping legalization of cannabis.
He's had a supermajority for the past 6
years, can pass whatever he wants, and
hasn't addressed those topics, and
again, has been on the other side. So,
again, what I'm fighting for, it's all
mainstream, and the numbers back it up.
>> And Kansas Reflector did report
September 18th that Senator Masterson
was not going to be part of future
debates on this. We'll see if that
changes. So, you touched on a lot of
things that I do plan to ask you about.
Let's get to data centers. It's a huge
issue right now we're seeing in rural
Kansas.
We're also seeing lithium-ion battery
concerns in Sumner County, south of us
solar projects. We've seen that here in
Sedgwick County.
But, the rural counties, Barber County
being really the latest one to give the
go-ahead to at least the next step with
a Google data center. But, also, we're
seeing this in some of the urban ones.
Lots of people turning around turning
out for this. The overwhelming vocal
opinion of this is no. If people are
supporting this, they're not making a
lot of noise about this. During the
debate, you talked about the data
center's contributions to your
opponent's campaign. But, you stopped
short of saying no on data centers, that
they need guardrails. Two-pronged
question for you Senator. Do you see
yourself ever being a hard no on data
centers?
And if governor, how would you stop them
if enough Republicans support them?
>> Yeah. We already have data centers out
there.
Uh a number of them have been built with
the appropriate guardrails. What we're
seeing though unfold across the nation,
and even here in Kansas, are the
entrance of these hyperscale data
centers
without always having those guardrails
in place. But, the bigger issue also
seems to be transparency. Some of these
deals are being rushed through, and
obviously that makes people in these
communities very, very anxious. I mean,
they want their seat at the table, and
we need to make sure that they have that
seat.
And what we're seeing here, you know,
lots of times we, you know, on the state
level will say, well, we need to respect
local control and I absolutely do and I
want local leaders to be able to make
decisions, but in this case they're
reaching out to us and saying, "Please
help us put these guardrails in place."
Because you have these data center
companies, these big tech companies
coming in, you know, with their
attorneys, their negotiators and often
on the local level they don't have those
types of resources. So, they are asking
us on the state level and as leaders, we
should be willing to step up by help put
those guardrails in place to protect
water, to protect energy usage and as
somebody from a union family, I want to
make sure those are good union jobs
because often these companies are
bringing in their crews from out of
state and we don't even get that
economic benefit. So, we just need to
make sure that we're helping our
communities get the deal that they're
envisioning because sometimes we're not
seeing that happen.
>> Taxes and revenue, Senator Masterson
said in the debate, quote, "She's for
the government every times." You talked
multiple times about
legalizing cannabis in Kansas and then
getting the revenue that would come off
of this. If you're governor and enough
Republicans joined you on this, do you
have an estimate for how much revenue
would come in from this?
>> Yeah, we need to revisit it a little bit
more closely, but in Missouri 255
million has been collected and
>> That's the same number I saw. So, yeah,
okay.
>> let's go back to that. I did help get
cannabis medicinal cannabis passed in
the house.
But who stopped it? It was Senator
Masterson in the Senate who stopped that
bill for moving forward and you know,
that was a couple of years ago. I
believe now that we have a growing
number of people who are interested in
this. If you go to state line and drive
by the dispensaries there, you're going
to find Kansas plates in the parking
lot. Some of my peers across the aisle,
Senator Masterson included, will say,
"Well, we don't want cannabis in
Kansas." It's already here. We're just
not getting the revenue and we don't
have our guardrails in place. It's
already here.
>> on that. Let's say it's $100 million
just by going by population numbers. If
you've got a state budget of 10, 11
billion dollars,
that's 1%. Is it worth what might be
some of the societal concerns that can
come from it? I know you just said,
"Well, it's already here in Kansas. But
when it comes to just addiction concerns
and how much that 100 million would have
to go back towards treatment anyway. I
mean it's it's
>> Sure.
>> because we're always looking to bring in
more revenue. I think you know, most
politicians are in some ways. But and
you clearly feel this is the right way,
but do you have concerns about societal
impact?
>> Well, as someone who has helped author
several of the bills in the past, you
put the appropriate guardrails in there
to address those issues. And at this
point, you know, I guess the good news
is with so many other states already
having a program in place, we can take
from the best models. So of course you
want to address those issues. But yeah,
at the heart of the matter, it will
bring in revenue. And if you take a look
at what we could do with that, we could
use it to fund special education which
hasn't been fully funded since 2011.
That's what's driving our property taxes
up. So we fund special education, then
it has an impact in other areas. So like
I said, yeah, there's definitely good
revenue there and it's already here.
We're not getting it.
>> Gas prices, I'm sure when you and your
staff are driving past there 419 right
there at the gas station. That's the
common price we're seeing right now as
we're taping this in Wichita September
20th. Diesel above $6 in a lot of spots.
So much more of these everyday items are
going to be more expensive even if
they're not already and we'll talk about
the affordability part.
Does this help your campaign even as
more people are having to dig further
into their pocket in these final weeks
until November? And I'm not saying this
in a in a
in a way where you obviously want that
to happen. But the high gas prices out
there, people link that to the current
administration. Does that help you out?
>> Well, I mean, the thing is
I'm very uncomfortable with where things
are because I know people are struggling
and then this is another area that's
making it more difficult you know, for
people to get by, to be able to pay
their bills.
When I see those gas prices going up, it
gives me a certain amount of anxiety
because I come from a family that didn't
have much. I know what that's like
trying to stretch and make those ends
meet. And like I said, it gives me a
certain amount of anxiety when I see
that happening because I know what's
happening to families out there. They're
trying to figure out, do I pay this
bill? Do I get my medication? Do I get
groceries?
Um
and sadly, we keep seeing more and more
policy like this from Washington, from
President Trump, who has endorsed my
opponent Ty Masterson.
So, have we seen Masterson pushing back
against these policies? No. So, what can
we expect? We can expect more of the
same if he becomes our governor. Where,
you know, there's a con- continuation of
catering to billionaires, of catering to
donors, not the people. I'm here to
serve the people, not the special
interest groups, not the billionaires.
I'm here to serve the people.
>> On affordability, 30-year fixed-rate
mortgage approaching 7% again. For
anyone who's gone to the grocery store
lately, I'm in it 3 days a week. Corned
beef up 15% and your lettuce 20%, coffee
even more than this.
So, we all see this, but what could you
do or propose as a governor, especially
if you're working with an unfriendly
party on the other side in the
legislature, to try to help with this?
>> I've had to work with plenty of
unfriendly parties. I mean, I'm in the
super minority and have been for 10
years and been able to get bills to the
finish line. So, can I educate others?
Yes, I can do that. Can I push back?
Absolutely. And that's what you will see
me doing. You will see me pushing back
against horrible policy as, you know,
the federal level tries to bring it in,
as the legislature tries to push policy
that is not good for Kansas. And you
will absolutely see me push back on that
and you will see me pulling forward
things that are good for the people.
>> Okay, so let's stay with this. How would
a Holchur
governorship differ from being Governor
Kelly's third term? Where would it be
different if if you win in November than
what we've seen for the last 8 years, at
least out of the governor's office?
>> Yeah. Well, again, I have this history
of being able to get things to the
finish line. So, I'm going to keep
working in that fashion to make sure
that we're delivering.
Um but I think again, the biggest
contrast isn't so much myself versus
previous governors. It's myself versus
my opponent. And like I said, you're
going to continue to see billionaire
giveaways,
uh tax deductions for corporations cuz
that's what he's been pushing these past
several years. And that's what me and a
small group of people have been pushing
back against.
>> Back to food for a second, but dairy
meat processing with immigration. It's a
big part of what we see in rural Kansas.
Now, you said in the debate in
Hutchinson back in the 12th, the Biden
White House did not take immigration
enforcement seriously. President Trump
is not doing it the right way. So, given
how prevalent this part
is in the Kansas economy for immigrants,
their lives, their jobs, and in our
viewing area, what do you see as the
right way on handling this?
>> Yeah. So, we need immigration reform. On
the and that comes from the federal
level. Now, I know this. We want our
border secure. You know, we don't want
criminals coming in. We don't want drugs
like fentanyl coming into our towns and
communities. So, we need immigration
reform. I will do everything I can to
work with our congressional delegation
to make sure that reform happens because
that's what we are needing and that's
what people are saying. But, I will tell
you what people don't like is they don't
like what they have seen from the Trump
administration and ICE in terms of
rounding up of people from meat packing
plants, law-abiding citizens who are
contributing to the economy. We want the
criminals focused on. Again, not the
people who are doing the work in the on
the farms or in the meat packing plants.
Again, the criminals is is where the
focus is needing to be.
>> Staying with labor, but just a different
facet. So, you mentioned using union
labor for major projects. You talked
about this at the State Fair debate.
Data centers, new Chief Stadium. US
Bureau of Labor Statistics that last
year in Kansas, about 6% of our
workforce in Kansas is part of a union.
So, you worked for Sprint in Kansas City
for for 12 years, and it was a major
company when it was in Kansas City
before it became part of T-Mobile. It
had a very documented past of is very
anti-union.
So, you know, we've all worked in places
where we may not agree with what the
boss does or what the corporation does.
I get that part of it. Was there a point
though whenever you were working there
and you said you come from a union
family where
you wish they would have been more
friendly to that cuz you were working in
marketing for that. So, you know, you
had to put the best face of the company
forward. Or was that something that also
evolved over time with you?
>> Yeah, I mean, I really wasn't involved
in that part. I mean, you know, that was
several years ago when I was working
there. I had a good career there. I
actually designed and implemented
budgets for large departments, uh which
is very much work pertinent to this job
as governor,
uh and working a very collaborative
fashion. So, like I said, I really
wasn't a part of that. What I will tell
you is the entire time I've been in the
legislature, my voting record for unions
has been 100%. I'm very focused to
making sure that we have livable wages
for our folks, and that we're using
union labor, uh because that is part of
my culture. And again, I want to make
sure these are livable wages, and that's
why the push is there.
>> And back to state legislature. So, it's
a place you know well, 4 years in the
house, uh from Olathe, 6 years in the
senate. Was there any major piece of
legislation that you feel the Republican
majority's got right, though? And if you
were the governor,
where could you work with them on some
parts?
>> Yeah. Well, I will speak to a couple
things there. I mean, obviously ending
the Brownback experiment, you know, had
to get a whole number of people on board
to make that happen. Again, with
Democrats being the minority, uh that
was tedious, but we got it done. My
opponent, when we ended that experiment,
my opponent said the bill to end the
Brownback experiment was a piece of
garbage, and said he thought the
Brownback experiment should go further.
That's what my opponent, Masterson,
said, that the Brownback experiment
didn't go far enough. That should be a
warning to all of us in terms of what a
governorship with him would be like. If
Brownback experiment didn't go far
enough, what would he unleash to us on
the state level? I mean, that's
absolutely concerning, because our
schools were struggling. We had nine
rounds of budget cuts.
Uh you know, our credit rating was was
downward. I mean, he bankrupted the
state. That's an absolute concern, and
in his view, it didn't go far enough.
So, there's one bill, like I said, that
I'm extremely proud of, that uh got
Republicans on board. I also did statute
of limitations reform for survivors of
sexual violence. That was a bill I
worked on that was groundbreaking
reform. I worked on it for 4 years.
Um it changes, you know, previously our
statutes were a bit outdated. So that if
someone
uh was violated as a child that they
only had a very narrow time frame in
which to bring forward their cases. That
time frame nowhere aligned with reality
of the fact that it takes decades often
for survivors to bring forward their
cases. So I worked on that issue.
Initially, there weren't a lot of people
in favor of it. They didn't understand
it, but I educated my peers.
Um I had a survivor group who came in
and also talked to my uh peers in the
legislature educating them on the topic.
And in the end, we passed that bill
unanimously in the house and the Senate.
Again, took a lot of work, but we got
everybody on board. So again, working
from the perspective of the minority
party,
I can get it done.
>> Public education. Just got a couple more
questions for you here.
On the same day the people are going to
decide if you're going to become our
next governor, voters in the Wichita
school district are deciding on a $615
million two-question bond issue. Wichita
school voters have not passed a bond in
since 2008. If you're governor,
how could you actually help with public
education still have the Republicans
right along with you on this one? Or is
there something that they could do that
you would sign off on and not be that
veto?
>> So 90% of our children attend public
schools. Uh
public school funding is absolutely
important to people in rural areas as
well as urban. So
uh you know, we have a good faction of
people who have been working together to
try to stop voucher programs which
defund our schools. My opponent Senator
Masterson has been uh pushing those in
efforts to defund public education. But
the story here unfortunately is that
while we have adequately funded general
education, as I mentioned earlier, we
have not fulfilled our obligation on
special ed funding. We haven't fulfilled
that obligation as a legislature since
2011. Now there's a group of us, myself
included, who've been pushing to get
special education fully funded because
here's what happens. When it isn't fully
funded, it hurts all our schools.
I mean,
it hurts schools here in Wichita, it
hurts schools all across the state when
special ed isn't fully funded because
then funds have to be diverted. So, in
the end, then what happens is that lack
of funding is pushed to the local level.
That makes property taxes go up. And we
have had a whole lot of talk about
property taxes the past few of year past
few years. My opponent has said that he
will deliver property tax relief.
There's two things that got to happen
there. We have to ensure general ed and
and special ed are fully funded. That
hasn't been happening. And these big
corporate giveaways have to stop
happening. These exemptions, grants to
corporations and billionaires. That has
to stop happening. My opponent is
nowhere on board with doing those
things. That's why property taxes go up.
And if you take a look, the past 6
years, while he has been Senate
President, he's had a super majority. He
can pass anything he wants. If he were
serious about property tax relief, we
would have it, but we don't. So, that
tells me he either doesn't know how to
solve it or doesn't want to. And you've
probably seen the ads out there. There's
ads saying Cindy Holscher voted against
property tax relief.
I'm one Democrat in the whole scheme of
things. Again, he's got a super
majority. I by myself can't stop his
property tax gimmicks that he's trying
to push. His own party rejected his
bills and his gimmicks cuz it doesn't
address the issue.
>> Rural hospitals, El Dorado,
25 minutes out of our studios in
Wichita. This summer, voters there
passed a sales tax for 7 years. All the
revenue going to the hospital there. And
hospital leaders called it at the time
during the campaign that it was
necessary just for survival. You and
your opponent were very split on
Medicaid expansion. We heard it again
during the state fair debate. You said
in the debate that hospitals are six
times more likely to close without
Medicaid expansion. Is there an opening
for you to win support by talking about
Medicaid expansion for the rural
hospitals, especially in these more
conservative, more Republican rural
counties that often do not vote for
Democrats in statewide elections?
>> Oh, absolutely. You know, our rural
communities don't want to lose their
hospitals. I come from a community that
lost a hospital. We know what it's like.
You have to drive further for care.
Additionally, you lose some of your best
jobs in the community. So, yes, there is
an opening there, and I do see the
opening and the pathway forward on it.
Because again, you're absolutely right.
Without Medicaid expansion, our
hospitals are six times more likely to
close, and we can't afford to lose any
more of those. We have forfeited Our
state has forfeited over $7 billion of
our tax funds that should be going here
to take care of our people and help our
communities and help us keep our
hospitals. That money's going to other
states because people like Ty Masterson
have opposed Medicaid expansion. We got
to move forward with this.
>> Senator Cindy Holscher, we thank you for
your time.
>> Yeah.
>> Telling us about your campaign, making
time for us here at the KAKE studios.
Safe travels for the final weeks of the
campaign.
>> Thank you. I appreciate it so much.
